net_router.name: Router installation & replacement
net_router.summary: Fit or swap the customer's gateway router so the whole property gets internet. The router takes the line from the ONT and shares it over Wi-Fi and Ethernet.
net_router.overview: The gateway router is the heart of every customer network. Its WAN port takes the internet from the fibre ONT. Every switch, access point, laptop, NVR and server in the building then gets online through it. A router on the wrong port, with no power or not cabled to a live ONT, leaves the customer with nothing — and their CCTV remote viewing, laptops and self-hosted websites go down with it.

equipment.name: Gateway router (OPS Gateway Pro / Mini, OPS EdgeLink E5 / E7, OPS HomeRouter AX4)
equipment.what: Routes traffic between the customer's LAN and the internet, hands out addresses (DHCP) and runs the firewall and Wi-Fi.
equipment.how: Placed as a Wi-Fi/router tower from the /towers menu. It must be powered (socket nearby or PoE) and cabled to the ONT to show as online.

equipment.name: Fibre ONT
equipment.what: Turns the light on the customer's fibre into Ethernet. It needs light from a cabinet and an active OPS Network service.
equipment.how: Usually already fitted on the wall. [E] shows its light and service status.

equipment.what: Connects the ONT LAN port to the router WAN port.
equipment.how: Pull CAT6 from the nearest box, then terminate one end on the ONT and the other on the router.

steps.title: Power on and check it's online

net_lan.name: LAN, Wi-Fi & PoE installation

net_lan.overview: Behind every router there's a local network. Switches add ports, PoE switches power access points and cameras down the cable, and access points spread Wi-Fi through the building. Good cabling makes it all reliable: runs under 100 m, terminated properly, labelled and tidy. A business installation is the full set: gateway, PoE switch, two access points and all the CAT6 between them.

net_support.name: Network fault finding & support
net_support.summary: Find out why a customer's internet is slow or down and put it right. Speed issues are signed off with a speed test that reaches 70% of the package.
net_support.overview: Most 'no internet' calls are one of four things: the ONT has no light (fibre fault), the line is suspended or unpaid, the router is unplugged or misconfigured, or Wi-Fi coverage is poor. Work from the outside in: the line on OPS Hub, then the ONT, the router, and the Wi-Fi. A speed job is finished when an OPS Work speed test at the property reaches at least 70% of the customer's package.

isp_install.name: New fibre broadband installation

When the ONT has light and the job is completed, OPS Network activates the line: it links the ONT, assigns public IP addresses, pushes the router settings and takes the first bill. If any link in that chain is missing, the customer gets nothing.

fibre_maint.name: Fibre testing & repair

us_osp.name: US outside plant construction & splicing
us_osp.summary: Build the outside plant: feeder and distribution fiber, FDHs, FDTs, aerial strand, handholes, vaults and splice closures.
us_osp.overview: Outside plant (OSP) is everything between the central office and the customer. Feeder fiber leaves the CO in high-count cables and runs to fiber distribution hubs (FDHs) — street cabinets holding passive splitters (1:8 up to 1:128) that share one PON port among many homes. Splitters need no power and do not switch traffic; they just divide the light. Distribution fiber continues from the FDH to fiber distribution terminals (FDTs) on poles or in pedestals, where drops are connected. Aerial plant uses utility poles: a steel messenger strand is placed between poles, held with anchors and guy wires, and the fiber is lashed to it. Underground plant uses conduit, handholes, vaults and manholes. Fibers are joined by fusion splicing inside splice closures, and every fiber is recorded in the network inventory and GIS so the NOC can trace any customer to the OLT port.

us_co.name: US central office & core network
us_co.summary: The active network: OLTs, ODFs, aggregation, BNGs, core and edge routers, CO power and cooling.
us_co.overview: The central office (CO) houses the active network. Outside-plant fiber terminates on the optical distribution frame (ODF), where it is patched to OLT PON ports. Each OLT port serves many homes through splitters and handles ONT authentication, bandwidth, service profiles and VLANs. OLT uplinks feed aggregation routers and switches, which collect traffic from many OLTs with redundant links so one failure does not take an area down. Broadband network gateways (BNGs) handle subscriber sessions, IP addresses and policies. Aggregation connects to the metro and core networks — high-capacity routers on 100–800 Gbit/s links, often over DWDM optical transport — and the internet edge routers exchange routes with transit providers, internet exchanges and content networks using BGP. All of this runs on DC power from rectifiers with battery strings and a standby generator, and cooling that keeps the room in range.

us_noc.name: US network operations (NOC)
us_noc.summary: Monitor the network and work alarms down to the fault — the NOC workflow.
us_noc.overview: The NOC watches every layer: access (ONTs, OLTs), aggregation, metro, core, optical transport, internet edge, data centres and power. Network management systems raise alarms when thresholds are crossed — ONTs offline, optical levels low, interfaces down, high temperature. When several customers on the same PON drop at once, the cause is shared: a fiber cut, damaged feeder or distribution cable, a failed splitter, an OLT port or card, or power. The NOC compares the affected customers using inventory, narrows it to a section, checks the OLT, and dispatches OSP with the location. After the fix, optical levels and ONTs are checked and the incident is closed.

sections.title: What it does
sections.body: Every phone call, text and bit of mobile data goes through OPS Mobile's masts. Each tower covers a radius; phones show bars based on the strongest tower in range. With Enforce on, no signal means no calls, texts or data.

sections.title: Masts and small cells
sections.body: Lattice masts and 5G masts are placed from /towers. They need power — a socket, a solar/battery set-up or the grid. A mast that loses power drops out and leaves a dead spot.

sections.title: Plans
sections.body: Players need an OPS Mobile plan (a free starter is given). Texts, minutes and data come from the plan; Wi-Fi from a router with internet doesn't use the plan.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.body: A mast on a feeder that loses power takes coverage with it. Gunshot sensors and trackers report over OPS Mobile too, so they stop reporting in dead spots.

sections.title: Where to look
sections.body: OPS Hub → Tower map shows every mast and its coverage; OPS Hub → Lines shows customers.

sections.title: From station to socket
sections.body: Power stations feed 400 kV transmission to substations, which step it down to 11 kV feeders, then pole transformers to LV, and a service drop to each property's cut-out and meter. The consumer unit then feeds sockets, lights and chargers.

sections.title: Substations
sections.body: A substation needs protection, a DC battery and earthing to energise. An RTU lets Grid control switch it remotely.

sections.title: Grid control
sections.body: OPS Hub → Grid control shows load, faults and switching. Feeders can trip on faults or be switched for maintenance.

sections.title: What depends on it
sections.body: Sockets, lighting, EV chargers, routers, ONTs, NVRs, masts, fuel pumps and data-centre UPS charging all need live mains. A feeder outage cascades: no power means no internet, CCTV or mobile signal unless there's battery backup.

sections.title: Safety
sections.body: Always isolate, lock off and prove dead before work. Never assume a circuit is dead.

sections.title: The exchange
sections.body: Exchanges house the OLT (fibre light source), the MDF (copper), core routers and power plant (rectifiers, batteries, generator).

sections.title: Out to the street
sections.body: Feeder fibre runs to street cabinets, then to distribution points (CBTs) on poles. Copper runs exchange → PCP cabinet → pole → house.

sections.title: Into the home
sections.body: A fibre drop ends in an ONT; a copper drop ends in a master socket (NTE). The ONT needs light from upstream and an active service.

sections.title: Faults
sections.body: Random network faults (water in joints, cracked enclosures, cut cables) take everything downstream offline and raise jobs. Several lines down together raise an outage.

sections.title: Underground
sections.body: Chambers, ducts and tunnels carry cables under roads. Lids are heavy and gas can build up — never work alone in one.

sections.title: Lines
sections.body: A line is a customer, a package and an ONT. Ordering raises an install job; completing it activates the line: ONT linked, public IPs assigned, router settings pushed, first bill taken.

sections.title: IP addresses
sections.body: Dynamic 203.0.113.0/24, static 198.51.100.0/24 and dedicated /29 blocks from 192.0.2.0/24. Static IPs let customers host their own servers.

sections.title: Router settings
sections.body: LAN, DHCP, DNS, Wi-Fi, VLANs, firewall, port forwards and VPN — edited on OPS Hub and pushed to the router in game.

sections.title: Monitoring
sections.body: Every 30 s line states are updated (up, degraded, down). Three or more lines down within 450 m opens an outage, notifies customers and raises an emergency job.

sections.title: Billing
sections.body: Every 7 days; unpaid lines are suspended after 3 days' grace (the ONT is cut off) and come back when paid.

sections.title: One operator, every layer
sections.body: There is no single US network company. OPS America plays a large US fiber operator that owns its access network end to end: customer premises, fiber access, PON, OLTs, aggregation, metro, core, internet edge, peering and transit, plus the OSS, BSS and NOC that run it.

sections.title: Customer premises
sections.body: The ONT terminates the fiber and hands Ethernet (1, 2.5 or 10 GbE) to the customer’s gateway, which does IPv4/IPv6, DHCP, NAT, firewall, routing and Wi-Fi. The ONT is tied to the subscriber in inventory and must be authorised by the OLT before service works.

sections.title: PON & splitters
sections.body: A passive optical network shares one OLT port among many homes through unpowered splitters (1:8 to 1:128). XGS-PON gives about 10 Gbit/s each way per PON; each customer’s speed is set by their service profile, not the PON total.

sections.title: Feeder, distribution & drop
sections.body: Feeder fiber runs from the central office to fiber distribution hubs (FDHs); distribution fiber runs to fiber distribution terminals (FDTs) on poles or in pedestals; the drop goes from the FDT to the house, aerially or buried in conduit.

sections.title: Outside plant
sections.body: Aerial plant hangs fiber lashed to messenger strand on utility poles, held with anchors and guy wires. Underground plant uses conduit, handholes, vaults, manholes and pedestals. Splice closures protect joins; slack is stored for repairs.

sections.title: Central office
sections.body: Fiber terminates on the ODF and is patched to OLT PON ports. OLTs uplink to aggregation routers and switches. DC power (rectifiers, batteries, generator) and HVAC keep it running; access control, CCTV and fire systems protect it.

sections.title: Aggregation, metro & core
sections.body: Aggregation collects many OLTs with redundant links. Metro networks join COs, data centres and edge sites. The core carries traffic between regions on 100–800 Gbit/s links, often over DWDM optical transport with ROADMs and amplifiers.

sections.title: BNG & internet edge
sections.body: BNGs handle subscriber sessions, IP addresses and policies. Edge routers connect to transit providers, internet exchanges and content networks using BGP; inside the network IS-IS or OSPF route traffic.

sections.title: OSS, BSS & the NOC
sections.body: OSS keeps the inventory, GIS, IPAM, provisioning and fault management; BSS handles orders, billing and customers. The NOC watches every layer and dispatches field techs. In OPS Hub these are the ISP pages, the maps, the Operations centre and Alerts.

sections.title: When it goes wrong
sections.body: One house down: check the ONT, optical power, connectors and drop. Many ONTs on one PON down together: the fault is shared — a fiber cut, damaged feeder or distribution cable, a failed splitter, an OLT port or power. The NOC traces it with inventory and sends OSP with an OTDR.

sections.title: Systems
sections.body: A system is a recorder (NVR or DVR) and its cameras. IP cameras use PoE over CAT6; analogue cameras need a DVR; wireless cameras need Wi-Fi and a powered NVR on site.

sections.title: Power & budgets
sections.body: The NVR has 8 PoE ports and a 120 W budget; PoE switches add more. A camera without power, a channel or a path stays offline.

sections.title: Recording & events
sections.body: Motion, heat, ANPR plate reads and doorbell rings are recorded as events. Recording modes are motion, continuous or off.

sections.title: Who can watch
sections.body: The owner, people they share with, members of an organisation job (e.g. police) and staff. Remote viewing needs the NVR online and remote viewing on.

sections.title: Faults
sections.body: Lens, cable and dead faults raise OPS Secure jobs. OPS Hub → CCTV systems shows everything live.

sections.title: Data halls
sections.body: Racks, UPS, generators and CRAC cooling within 25 m form a hall. Racks need power (UPS or socket), a ToR switch and a CAT6 uplink to an online router.

sections.title: Heat
sections.body: Running servers make heat; CRAC units remove 30 kW each. Over 32 °C servers degrade; at 40 °C they shut down until it cools.

sections.title: Power
sections.body: On mains the UPS charges; in a power cut it runs on battery (longer at low load), then everything goes dark.

sections.title: OPS Cloud
sections.body: Customer VMs are placed on healthy 'cloud' role hosts in their region, restarted elsewhere when a host dies, or left 'host down' / 'waiting for capacity'.

sections.title: Platform roles
sections.body: Servers can run OPS Web hosting, OPS DNS or OPS mail. Once a role has servers, that service is down whenever none is reachable — websites time out, lookups fail, mail bounces.

systems.name: The in-game internet: domains, websites, DNS, email & SSL

sections.title: The Browser
sections.body: A real web for the city, on phones (mobile data) and laptops (Ethernet). ops.sa is OPS Search.

sections.title: Domains
sections.body: Registered at opsdomains.sa (.ls .sa .biz .shop .club; .gov.sa for government). They renew from the owner's bank, expire, then are released after a grace period.

sections.title: DNS
sections.body: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and TXT records decide where a name goes. 198.18.10.80 is OPS Web hosting; a customer's static or cloud IP self-hosts.

sections.title: Websites
sections.body: Built from blocks at opsweb.sa — never raw HTML, so no player code runs on anyone's phone. Live when published and the DNS points at the server.

sections.title: HTTPS & email
sections.body: Certificates from OPS Trust CA (free DV with hosting). No valid certificate means 'Not secure' or a full-page warning. Mailboxes deliver into the phone's Mail app; unknown addresses bounce.

sections.title: What it is
sections.body: GPS trackers fitted in vehicles: live position, theft alerts and an immobiliser on Pro units.

sections.title: How it reports
sections.body: Over OPS Mobile. With no signal it stores positions and sends them when signal returns.

sections.title: Owners
sections.body: /track lists your vehicles, locates them and arms theft alerts.

sections.title: Staff
sections.body: /towers → OPS Track to install, test and remove; OPS Hub → Vehicle tracking shows the live map.

sections.title: Stations
sections.body: Underground or bunded tanks, automatic tank gauges, dispensers, a canopy, an emergency stop, a tanker fill point and vent stacks.

sections.title: Power
sections.body: Dispensers need power; in a power cut the pumps stop.

sections.title: Deliveries
sections.body: Tankers refill tanks at the fill point.

sections.title: Safety
sections.body: Fuel vapour ignites easily — no sparks, phones or smoking near open fuel.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Panels → DC isolator → hybrid inverter → consumer unit, with a home battery beside the inverter.

sections.title: Day and night
sections.body: In daylight the panels power the house and charge the battery. After dark, or in a power cut, the battery takes over.

sections.title: Limits
sections.body: Panels must be within 30 m of the inverter; the inverter feeds the consumer unit beside it.

sections.title: Checking
sections.body: [E] on the inverter shows output and battery charge.

sections.title: A job's life
sections.body: Open → accepted (a snapshot of the world is taken) → the work is done for real → checked against the world → the customer pays → the company is credited → you're paid wages → an invoice is issued.

sections.title: Quotes & contracts
sections.body: Quotes become work orders when accepted. Contracts bill every period and set response times (SLA). Support contracts make repairs free.

sections.title: SLA
sections.body: Each job gets a due time: from the contract, the customer's tier (critical 4 h, premium 8 h, business 24 h, standard 72 h) or 4 h for emergencies. Late finishes are breaches on the dashboards.

sections.title: Stock, assets & warranty
sections.body: Completed jobs use parts from stock. Kit fitted is registered to the customer with a serial and warranty — warranty repairs are free. Low stock raises alerts; purchase orders restock.

sections.title: Tickets & alerts
sections.body: Customers raise tickets from the phone or the portal. Alerts cover stock, SLA, contracts, certifications and vans.

systems.name: Training, certification, safety & the job assistant

sections.title: Certifications
sections.body: Each job family has a course: classroom lessons, a safety module, an exam and (if enabled) an in-game practical at the OPS Academy. Installation work needs the family's certification to be accepted.

sections.title: The job assistant
sections.body: On any job, 'Guide me' (or /jobhelp) shows the next step, the tools you need and where to get them, the safety controls and what goes wrong if you skip steps.

sections.title: Risk assessment
sections.body: Before on-site work you confirm a dynamic risk assessment: PPE, cones, isolation, ladder or harness. Skipping it on risky work can cause accidents (falls, shocks) and is logged.

sections.title: Standalone or items
sections.body: In standalone mode your van has the tools and kit comes from /towers. In items mode tools and parts are inventory items collected from an OPS depot, and jobs use them up.

sections.title: Configuration
sections.body: Everything — systems on/off, companies, jobs, prices, timings — can be changed in the config files, OPS Hub → Settings / Jobs / Companies, or OPS Work → Admin.

config.name: Configuring OPS
config.desc: Every way to change how the OPS systems work — files, OPS Hub and the phone — and what each setting group does.

slides.title: Three ways to configure everything
body: The config files: opslabs-towers/config.lua, opslabs-phone/config.lua, opslabs-phone/sql/ops_catalog.json and sql/ops_guides.json.
OPS Hub → Settings, Jobs, Companies: every value, with its explanation, saved in the database.
OPS Work → Admin settings on the phone: the most-used switches, every job and every company.
What wins: a value set on OPS Hub or the phone overrides the file. "Reset" puts it back to the file’s value.

slides.title: What lives where
body: opslabs-towers/config.lua — mobile masts and Wi-Fi, cabling, mains electricity, the power grid, solar, fuel, OPS Track, the ISP, CCTV, data centres, gunshot sensors, faults, buildings, roadworks, lighting, vans.

opslabs-phone/config.lua — the phone itself, OPS Mobile plans, the OPS platform (automatic jobs), Features (web, cloud, business, training, assistant) and Work (play mode, depots, safety, training, animations).
sql/ops_catalog.json — companies, roles and permissions, job types, customer places, ISP pools, domain/hosting/cloud prices, stock lines, suppliers, contracts and SLA tiers.
sql/ops_guides.json — the training and job-assistant content: steps, tools, safety, mistakes, quizzes, exams and the classroom explainers.
config_server.lua — secrets (API keys, logins). Never shown on OPS Hub.

slides.title: OPS Hub → Settings
body: Quick settings: play mode, every system on/off, automatic jobs and the safety & training rules.
The two full editors list every setting of opslabs-towers and opslabs-phone as a tree. Search by name or by what it does — each one shows the comment from the config file.

Changes are saved straight away and applied in game within about 15 seconds. A few values are read when a script starts (for example turning a whole system on or off) — those apply on the next restart.
Every change is in the Platform audit log with who made it.

slides.title: Jobs editor
body: Switch any job type on or off, change the customer price and the engineer’s wage, decide whether it appears on its own, if it can be an emergency, the certification it needs, whether warranty/contracts make it free.
Parts: which stock items the job uses up (e.g. {"cat6": 20, "rj45": 2}).

The check (advanced): how the game proves the work was done — time on site, kit fitted, cable laid, ONT online, dial tone, live supply, cameras online, speed test, router settings, websites, data centre…
Create your own job types for any company: they appear in OPS Work within 30 seconds.

slides.title: Companies editor
body: Edit any company’s name, tagline, colour, icon, VAT and wage share.
Switch a company off: it disappears from OPS Work, gets no jobs and can’t be booked — handy if your server doesn’t want OPS Fuel or solar.
Create new companies, then give them job types in the Jobs editor and roles in Roles & permissions.

slides.title: Prices & catalogue
body: Settings → Prices & catalogue edits whole catalogue sections as JSON: domain endings and prices, hosting and cloud plans, certificate prices, stock lines and suppliers, SLA tiers and contract types, roles, the customer places that get automatic jobs.
OPS Hub uses them at once. The game writes them into sql/ops_catalog.json on start — restart opslabs-phone and opslabs-towers to use them.

slides.title: Play modes: standalone or items
body: Standalone (default): no inventory items needed. Tools are assumed to be in the van; kit is placed from /towers.

Items: tools, PPE and parts are inventory items. Engineers collect them at an OPS depot (Work.Depots) for the jobs they’ve accepted; jobs need their tools to start and use up their parts; placing kit from /towers uses its item (Work.ModelItems).
Add the items to your inventory first: opslabs-phone/items/ has ready-made definitions for ox_inventory, ESX and QBCore.

slides.title: Training & certification settings
body: Features.Training switches the whole training system on/off.

Work.RequireSafetyTraining: the family’s safety module before taking its jobs. Work.RequirePractical: an in-game practical at an OPS Academy centre (Work.TrainingCentres) as part of each certification. Work.PassMark: the pass mark for quizzes and exams.
Per job: the Jobs editor decides which certification a job needs and whether it’s required.
Content (lessons, steps, quizzes) is in sql/ops_guides.json — edit it to change what’s taught.

slides.title: Health & safety settings
body: Work.SafetyBriefing: a dynamic risk assessment before on-site work and before completing a job.
Work.SafetyIncidents: skip controls on risky work and accidents can happen (falls, shocks) — logged as safety incidents and alerted to managers.
Work.Anims: the animation used for each step type (dict/clip or scenario).

slides.title: Switching systems off
body: Each big system has an Enabled switch: Mains, Grid, OpsIsp, Cctv, DataCentre, Track, Fuel, Gunshot, Faults (opslabs-towers) and Features.* plus Carrier.Enabled (opslabs-phone).
Turning a system off stops its engine on the next restart; its jobs stay available unless you also switch them off in the Jobs editor (or switch the company off).
Enforce (opslabs-towers) decides whether phones need real tower signal.

slides.title: Good habits
body: Change one thing at a time and watch the game for a minute.
Use "Reset" to go back to the file’s value; the audit log shows every change.
Keep a copy of your config files before big edits, and test risky changes on a copy of the server.

firstjob.name: Your first OPS job
firstjob.desc: From signing in to getting paid — what an engineer does, step by step.

slides.title: Sign in and join a company
body: Open OPS Work on your phone, create an account and apply to a company. A manager approves you and gives you a role.

slides.title: Get trained
body: OPS Work → Training (or here in the Classroom): read the lesson, pass the health & safety module, pass the exam, and — if your server uses them — do the practical at the OPS Academy. Installation jobs need the certificate.

slides.title: Pick a job
body: Your company’s job board lists open work with the real address, the customer, the wage and the SLA deadline. Accept one — the GPS is set for you.

slides.title: Guide me
body: On the job page tap "Guide me" (or type /jobhelp): your next step, the tools you need and where to get them, the safety controls and what goes wrong if you skip steps.

slides.title: Risk assessment
body: Before work, tick the controls you really have in place — PPE, cones, isolation, ladder or harness. Skipping them on risky work can hurt you.

slides.title: Do the real work
body: Fit the kit from /towers, run and crimp the cable, configure on OPS Hub — whatever the job needs. Only work done after you accepted counts. The Work check on the job page shows your progress live.

slides.title: Complete and get paid
body: When the check passes, tap Complete. The customer pays (or warranty/contract covers it), the company is credited, you’re paid your wage and an invoice is issued. Finishing late counts as an SLA breach.
